name: Offensive Security
guide:
Offensive security professionals get paid to break things on purpose. Day to day the work is penetration testing against networks, applications and cloud infrastructure, plus red team engagements that simulate a real attacker chaining multiple weaknesses together to reach a goal. That is a different job from Application and Product Security, which builds secure software and reviews code before it ships, and different again from Vulnerability Management, which tracks, prioritizes and drives remediation of known flaws across an inventory of systems. Offensive security finds new ways in, Application Security prevents them at design time, and Vulnerability Management manages the backlog once flaws are already known. Readers job hunting under a general security title should check which of these three a posting actually means before applying.

On credentials, our tracked postings do not list specific certification names in their skill tags, so we cannot confirm from this database which of OSCP, OSCE or CEH employers here are actually asking for. Those three remain widely recognized names in the offensive security field generally, but that is general industry knowledge rather than something we can verify against the 20 postings in our sample. Degrees show up rarely as a gating requirement in this discipline compared to fields like data science. What tends to move a hiring decision is demonstrated hands on skill, a portfolio of findings, competition results or a track record of engagements, more than a diploma on file.

Experience requirements track seniority tightly in this sample. Ten of the twenty postings we pulled are mid level roles, the largest single group, at companies including OpenAI, Anthropic and Palantir. Two postings are senior, two are manager track, and six sit at staff or lead level split across Perplexity, Samsara, Scale AI, Nebius and Anthropic. Junior offensive security hires are rare in this sample, which suggests most employers here want someone who can run an engagement with limited supervision from day one rather than train a newcomer.

The skill tags attached to these postings lean heavily on cloud and systems knowledge rather than named exploitation tools. Python appears most often, followed by AWS, Red Teaming and Rust, with Kubernetes, Azure, GCP, Application Security, Cloud Security, CI/CD and Threat Modeling also recurring. Large Language Models and Model Evaluation show up repeatedly too, reflecting how many of these postings sit inside AI labs testing their own models and agent products for exploitable behavior. Classic penetration testing tools such as Metasploit, Burp Suite or Cobalt Strike did not appear as tags in this particular sample, though that likely reflects how the postings were tagged rather than what the job actually requires day to day.

On the market itself, in our own database we currently track approximately 13 open Offensive Security postings as of the most recent data pull, drawn from a broader sample of 20 postings we analyzed across recent history. Only one of those 20 postings carried salary figures, an Offensive Security Engineer role at Palantir Technologies in Washington, D.C. listing 151,052 dollars per year. That single data point is too thin to state a meaningful salary range for the discipline, so we are stating it honestly rather than dressing up one number as a market rate. The employers appearing most often in our tracked postings are OpenAI and Anthropic with three postings each, Palantir with three postings across its listings, and Scale AI and Samsara with two apiece, a mix that points to frontier AI labs as a significant current source of demand for this discipline alongside more traditional enterprise security teams.

reading.body:
Offensive security roles at major AI labs and infrastructure companies have become a distinct hiring category, with 14 active job postings across OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity, Palantir, and others as of September 2026.

The concentration of these roles at frontier AI companies reflects a shift in how compute-intensive organizations manage risk. Red team engineers and offensive security specialists probe systems for vulnerabilities before deployment, which becomes more critical as AI models control higher-stakes functions and consume greater resources. The volume and specificity of postings suggest these companies now treat adversarial testing as a core operational function rather than an occasional audit.

Most roles permit remote work, distributed across US tech hubs and Europe. The job titles vary between "Red Team Engineer," "Offensive Security Engineer," and "Red Team Specialist" without clear standardization, indicating the field is still establishing its boundaries. This data captures only posted positions and does not reflect hiring velocity, offer acceptance rates, or whether these roles directly impact infrastructure decisions.
